name: Green Beige
lede: Green Beige is a muted tan with a faint greenish cast, standardized by the German RAL system in 1927 as RAL 1000 and common enough in old paintings to show up in roughly one in nine.

sections.title: A standard beige
sections.body:
RAL 1000, issued in 1927, is the source for Green Beige here; the hex value is an approximation of the printed swatch on screen [1]. Despite the name, it reads to the eye mostly as a grayish yellow, filed by the ISCC-NBS system under that label; the "green" is a slight coolness rather than a visible green [2]. In Munsell terms it sits near 3.7Y 7.5/3.9: light, low chroma, barely tipped off true yellow [2].

The nearest named colors are [[sand|Sand]], 2.5 units away and almost identical, and [[very-light-brown|Very Light Brown]], 3.4 units away and also close [2]. RAL's own naming convention favors plain descriptive words over flower or place names, which is why this one reads as a compound rather than a story [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Green Beige appears in 2,603 of our 23,781 paintings, as photographed — about 11 percent, making it more common than 94 percent of the archive's named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1700s, and Arnoud van Halen is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 22 of his 50 works here, 4.4 times the baseline for his museums [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light [3]. The earliest match is dated 799, 1,128 years before RAL's 1927 standard — the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor on how far back the look-alike hue goes, not proof of any pigment [3].
